title: Paper 1 Q4: Points Make Prizes Explained
author: Mr Salles
source: Mr Salles Teaches English, Substack, July 19, 2026
summary: This article demonstrates the Points Make Prizes method for achieving top marks on AQA GCSE English Paper 1 Question 4 by dissecting a real student answer that progressed from 16/20 to a perfect 20/20. The central insight is that AQA examiners award one mark per valid explanation of reader effect—what the reader thinks, feels, or predicts—regardless of how the vague mark-scheme language frames success. The mark scheme uses entirely subjective terms like perceptive, convincing, and judicious, none of which are defined, which accounts for Ofqual's finding that 50% of English answers receive the wrong grade. Mr Salles verified this pattern through personal experience: sitting the exam twice and appealing marked responses, he confirmed that every mark rejection came down to whether the examiner agreed with an explanation. The article also clarifies a key structural point: detailed means quantity of reader-effect explanations, not depth, and some explanations should zoom in on individual words to provide a second interpretation of the same quotation.
points: AQA examiners award one mark per valid explanation of reader effect (think, feel, predict)—the number of valid explanations equals the number of marks, regardless of the mark scheme's vague criteria about being perceptive or convincing.

The mark scheme's subjective language has zero definitions, contributing to Ofqual's finding that 50% of GCSE English answers are incorrectly graded; Mr Salles confirmed this through two successful exam appeals.

Every rejection from senior examiners came down to disagreement with a specific explanation—never to the absence of explanations—proving that marks hinge on whether the examiner agrees, not on whether enough explanations were offered.
Detailed in Q4 means a large quantity of reader-effect explanations, not a single deep analysis; the model 20/20 answer provided six distinct reader-effect points across four quotes.

Some explanations should zoom in on individual words to offer a second reader-effect interpretation of the same quote—but doing only this type of explanation, without broader reader-effect points, will not yield full marks.
quotes: The student who wrote this piece kept getting stuck at 16/20 (which is still a grade 9). After reading my explanation, she scored 20/20 on her next question 4.

Every single word in bold is a judgement call. There are zero definitions of any of them in the mark scheme. Examiners are not given specific ways to decide on any of them. This is why 50% of English exam answers are given the wrong grade, according to Ofqual.
I’ve read every single answer AQA has published from a senior examiner. They all conform to this pattern - the number of valid explanations is the number of marks given to the answer.
I’ve sat the exam twice and got remarked twice. Then I appealed any reading question where I scored less than 100%.

Every reason they had for not awarding a mark was about whether they agreed with an explanation. In other words, the examiner completely ignored the fact that explanations are not mentioned in the mark scheme.
Many teachers believe this is the only kind of explanation that creates a detailed and perceptive response. It isn’t. Detailed means lots of explanations.
